"Orotund" is an adjective with two meanings that are closely related. Think of them as two sides of the same coin — one is about sound, and the other is about style of language. Here they are:
Meaning 1: A voice that is full, rich, and resonant

When you describe someone's voice as orotund, you mean it is round, deep, powerful, and impressively full. It is the kind of voice that fills a room without effort — the kind that makes people stop and pay attention just from the sheer quality of the sound itself. Think of a great stage actor, a seasoned preacher, or an old-school radio announcer. Their voices don't crack, don't thin out, don't trail off. They boom and flow with a certain grandeur.

An orotund voice is not just loud. A person can shout and have a terrible, scratchy voice. Orotund is about richness and resonance — the way the sound feels full and rounded, almost like it wraps around you. It's the voice equivalent of a deep, warm cello versus a thin, reedy whistle.

Example: "The actor walked onto the stage, and when he spoke, his orotund voice carried effortlessly to every corner of the theatre."
Meaning 2: Language that is pompous, inflated, and overly grand

This is the more widely used meaning today, and it carries a mildly negative flavour.

When writing or speech is called orotund, it means the language is overblown — unnecessarily grand, elaborate, and self-important. The person is using big, fancy, high-sounding words and sweeping phrases not because the content demands it, but because they want to seem impressive. The style has more hot air than substance. It's language that is puffed up beyond what the situation calls for.

Imagine a local politician giving a short speech about fixing a pothole, but doing so as if they were announcing the salvation of humanity — using sweeping declarations, soaring phrases, and grandiose vocabulary. That speech would be orotund. The content is small; the packaging is ridiculously large.

Example: "His orotund speeches were full of dramatic flourishes and lofty declarations, yet when you looked past all the grand language, he was really just saying very little."

You can see why these two meanings live in the same word. Both involve something being puffed up and round:

  • An orotund voice is physically round and full in sound.
  • Orotund language is stylistically bloated and round in the same way — swelled up with grandeur.

In both cases, the word captures this quality of something being impressively large and full — though in the case of language, that fullness often comes at the expense of genuine meaning.

When you call a voice orotund, you are usually paying it a compliment — it implies power, richness, and a kind of noble quality.

When you call someone's language or writing orotund, you are usually being gently critical — you are suggesting they are overdoing it, performing importance rather than communicating clearly. It is a sophisticated, slightly wry insult. It's more diplomatic than saying "they talk nonsense," but the implication is similar: all that grand sound, not enough real content.
When would you actually use this word?

You would use "orotund" when ordinary words like "rich," "deep," "pompous," or "pretentious" don't quite capture the specific quality you're describing — that particular combination of grandness and roundness of expression.

It's a word more at home in literary criticism, book reviews, political commentary, and thoughtful writing than in casual conversation. If a reviewer writes "the senator's orotund rhetoric masked a complete absence of policy," they are being precise and pointed in a way that "pompous" alone wouldn't fully achieve.
Quick mental image to remember it

Whenever you see or hear orotund, picture a big, round, ornate hot air balloon. It is impressively large, beautifully decorated, and floats majestically — but it is filled with nothing but air. That is exactly the spirit of orotund language. And if that balloon were somehow given a voice, deep and booming and resonant — that would be an orotund voice.
